lesson.title: Redox Reactions: Trading Electrons to Move Energy Around
lesson.summary: Oxidation and reduction always happen together as electrons move from one atom or molecule to another, and this electron traffic is how cells extract usable energy from food and capture energy from sunlight.
lesson.body:
A redox reaction is any reaction that transfers one or more electrons from one chemical species to another. Oxidation is the loss of electrons, and reduction is the gain of electrons, often remembered through the mnemonic OIL RIG: oxidation is losing, reduction is gaining. These two processes are inseparable, because an electron that leaves one atom has to land somewhere else. The substance that loses electrons is oxidized and is called the reducing agent, because it hands electrons to, and thereby reduces, its partner. The substance that gains electrons is reduced and is called the oxidizing agent.

To understand why electrons move at all, it helps to go back to the covalent bonds that hold biological molecules together. In a covalent bond, two atoms share a pair of electrons, but they rarely share equally, because different elements have different electronegativities, a property rooted in atomic structure, specifically how strongly a nucleus pulls on shared electrons. Carbon bonded to hydrogen shares electrons fairly evenly, but carbon bonded to oxygen does not, because oxygen is more electronegative and pulls the shared electrons closer to itself. Biochemists track oxidation this way: a carbon atom is more oxidized as it forms more bonds to electronegative atoms like oxygen, and more reduced as it forms more bonds to hydrogen. This is why converting a molecule rich in carbon hydrogen bonds, such as glucose, toward carbon dioxide, where carbon bonds only to oxygen, counts as oxidation of the carbon skeleton, even though no bare electron is seen floating freely between molecules.

In cells, electrons removed during oxidation are rarely transferred alone. They usually travel attached to hydrogen atoms or as part of a hydride ion, carried by dedicated electron carriers. The most important of these is nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, NAD+, which accepts two electrons and one proton to become NADH, with a second proton released into solution. Flavin adenine dinucleotide, FAD, similarly accepts two electrons and two protons to become FADH2. These carriers shuttle high energy electrons from one part of metabolism to another, most importantly from food breakdown to the electron transport chain.

Cellular respiration is built almost entirely out of a sequence of redox reactions. As glucose is processed through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the citric acid cycle, its carbon backbone is progressively oxidized, and the electrons removed at each stage reduce NAD+ and FAD to NADH and FADH2. Those reduced carriers donate their electrons to the electron transport chain, where the electrons pass through a series of protein complexes, alternately oxidized and reduced at each step, before finally reducing molecular oxygen to water. Oxygen's strong pull for electrons is why it works as the final electron acceptor and why aerobic respiration extracts far more energy than fermentation does. Photosynthesis runs a comparable strategy in reverse: water is oxidized to release electrons and oxygen gas, those electrons reduce NADP+ to NADPH, and NADPH's electrons ultimately reduce carbon dioxide into glucose in the Calvin cycle.

Seen this way, redox chemistry moves energy through metabolism, while free energy changes describe how favorable each transfer is. Electrons naturally move from molecules that hold them loosely toward molecules that hold them more tightly, releasing energy along the way, and cells have evolved carrier systems and enzyme complexes to capture that energy in usable forms rather than letting it simply dissipate as heat.
